Casey, an after-school program teacher in New York who asked to be referred to by a pseudonym, says she’s noticed many students’ parents, nannies, and other caretakers are now turning to ChatGPT or Claude for their questions on childhood development.

# Nobody is safe from celebrity AI deepfakes

AI photos and videos of celebrities are racking up millions of views on social media.﻿

In hindsight, the post on Instagram should have raised more red flags. The image purported to show actress Mia Goth , just days after filing for divorce from actor and filmmaker Shia LaBeouf, posing in a T-shirt with a pointed message: MY EX IS MY BIGGEST FAN . To really drive home the point, the song “Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)” by Beyoncé was added to the post.

It would have been out of character for the star of Pearl , who doesn’t have much of a social media presence, if any. But the Instagram account that posted it, @miagoth_, had more than a million followers and was marked with a blue “verified” checkmark. Within days, the image racked up nearly 500,000 likes, including from peers in the entertainment industry, despite the page being labeled as a fan account.

The image, as The Verge reported , was AI-generated, posted by an account Goth’s representative said they’d complained to Instagram about before for posting “counterfeit, AI images” of Goth. Meta allows users to purchase blue “verified” checkmarks , even if the account is not run by a prominent figure or isn’t an official page.

“The fact that this fan account meets Instagram’s criteria to qualify for a ‘blue check’ is disconcerting on a fundamental level,” Christine Tripicchio, a representative for Goth, told The Verge in an email. “Beyond that, it is incomprehensible that Instagram evidently prioritizes the dissemination of forged and manipulated images over the protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.”

### Related

- It’s ‘incomprehensible’ that Instagram allowed an AI image of Mia Goth to spread, say her reps

- Scarlett Johansson told OpenAI not to use her voice — and she’s not happy they might have anyway

Because of the news of her divorce, the post trickled through the celebrity gossip outlets, and that coverage in turn propagated the post through Google search. Searches for the actress and the shirt triggered an AI-generated overview saying Goth was taking “a clear swipe at her ex, Shia LaBeouf, following their recent divorce filing,” in turn citing the aforementioned blogs. A section in Google search results labeled “Mia Goth turns heads on Instagram by wearing a sassy ‘My ex is my biggest fan’ t-shirt” was featured prominently, along with links to social media posts discussing the image. Instagram eventually removed the account for impersonating a public figure.

Since consumer generative AI tools became available several years ago, some of the more memorable — and controversial — use cases have involved famous people. The human subjects in question have historically not responded well to being digitally cloned and used as playthings: An AI-generated Drake sound-alike song was wiped from YouTube following copyright strikes. Scarlett Johansson hired a legal team after OpenAI released a voice for ChatGPT that sounded like her without her consent. Ariana Grande is said to have blocked an account posting AI-generated content of her last year. Taylor Swift publicly endorsed Kamala Harris for president in 2024, saying she was moved to clarify her position after Donald Trump posted fake images suggesting she endorsed him .

There was a moment when everyone, even the rich and famous, was grappling with norms around a new technology. Now, the trough of AI content online is only growing — and it’s not clear if anyone is trying or able to stop it.

AI content depicting female public figures is often overtly sexual. A profile that exclusively posts AI-generated images of Johansson — often with bare feet prominently displayed — included contact information so that companies could advertise on the account, along with links to Patreon and Telegram channels selling subscriptions. The content off-platform used Johansson’s name and (AI) image to advertise adult content. Another account posts realistic AI-generated images of actors and musicians like Millie Bobby Brown, Zendaya, and Grande, always partially undressed or in sexualized positions. Some accounts have their own niche, like “ Stranger Things actors getting married to each other .”

After The Verge asked Meta about eight accounts posting celebrity deepfake content, spokesperson Alex Dziedzan said the company had removed some of the accounts . Two of them — the Goth one and the Johansson one — appear to be taken down.

“We do not permit accounts to use someone’s likeness to pose as that individual, regardless of whether the content is authentic or AI-generated,” Dziedzan said in an email.

Taylor Swift is holding a drink, rapping along to Drake’s “Burning Bridges,” expletives and all. “I’m off a [Quaalude]/it make my body tingle,” she sings, wearing the dress from the fateful 2009 VMAs moment . The video is AI, obviously. It has 1.8 million views on Instagram.

“I don’t think her pr team gonna like her saying the N word,” someone commented.

Instagram is filled with videos like this, often inexplicably following very specific formats. A clip of AI Shrek doing the same thing as AI Swift has 3.1 million views. Here’s Steve Jobs , swaggering around to a different Drake song with a bottle of champagne in his hand (371,000 views). There’s also an identical Lionel Messi version (2.1 million views) posted by a different account. Here are Formula 1 drivers Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen lipsyncing to “APT” by Bruno Mars and Rosé (2.9 million views). Another clip shows AI Swift’s wedding to AI Travis Kelce at AI Madison Square Garden.

“ai he wore white tuxedo,” one fan helpfully fact-checked.

In the absence of national right of publicity laws , AI-generated content featuring real people is being litigated on the platform level. (The US’s Take It Down Act, which was signed into law in 2025, specifically criminalizes the distribution of nonconsensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated content, and compels platforms to remove it within 48 hours.)

YouTube has likeness detection , perhaps the most robust deepfake monitoring and takedown system. Under the program, YouTube will scan its platform for visual matches for a person — and as of recently, sound-alikes — and allow them to request takedowns of content. Not every takedown request is accepted; the company says it considers public interest, newsworthiness, and consent in evaluating takedowns. The program was initially opened to public figures like celebrities, content creators, politicians, and journalists, but now covers every adult with a YouTube account . In the past, the company has said that the number of takedown requests it receives is relatively small. Creators want to be aware of what’s been posted of them on YouTube, but it often ends up being “fairly benign or additive to their overall business,” Amjad Hanif, vice president of creator products, said in a press briefing in March .

Still images are exempt from Meta’s AI labeling requirement

YouTube spokesperson Jack Malon noted in an email to The Verge that the company’s likeness detection was developed in partnership with the entertainment industry. Malon said that in the first half of 2026, YouTube removed over 95 percent of the videos that were reported through the program for takedowns.

AI-generated content on Meta platforms often has labels identifying it as such. Some content, like realistic videos of people or audio of AI-generated voices, is required to have an AI label. Still images, on the other hand, are exempt from the labeling requirement — meaning that the fake image of Mia Goth wouldn’t have required a disclosure under Meta’s rules. The company also introduced “AI-generated profile” labels that apply to an entire account where the avatar depicted doesn’t exist in the real world after an influx of AI influencer types flooded the platform.

But there is a cottage industry of accounts that pump out AI-generated imagery of real people that the algorithm seems to like. Some of the content isn’t obviously nefarious, just kind of strange: There’s a genre on Facebook, for example, of AI-generated movie premiere videos where the original cast (in costume) walks the red carpet next to actors for a recast version. One profile advertises $29-per-month online courses on how to make money through AI content.

AI-generated celebrity content also has the capacity to truly trick people into thinking it’s real, as in the case of the image (and account) depicting Goth. The specific post that went viral suggested the actress was taunting LaBeouf, who has been accused of abuse by another ex-partner and was filmed in 2015 saying he “would have killed [Goth]” if he had continued to argue with her. The fake image was attention-grabbing, shady, and timely — in other words, perfect for social media virality but a potential liability for the parties involved. The incident illustrates the failures of trust and safety provisions that are supposed to protect against this kind of confusion.

On social media, AI content mingles freely with standard-issue reposts of real images. And even when one page is taken down, there are others that continue to push out content: Another Instagram account — still live — with over 300,000 followers posts a steady stream of pictures and videos of Johansson, which appear to be a mix of authentic images and AI-generated content. One of its most popular posts is what looks to be an AI image of Johansson with nearly half a million likes. There is no AI disclosure, in line with Meta’s rules. The deepfaked Johansson lies on a couch, bare feet displayed prominently. It is not her, obviously — but her fans in the comments either don’t know or don’t care.

# AI agents are ready to shop. Some retailers are wary

AI agents are getting blocked left and right — but even when they work, it suggests a more annoying future for humans.

Using an AI agent to shop for you is a strange experience. Tech companies have marketed them as personal assistants — the democratizing of labor that ordinarily would only be available to the rich and powerful. In practice, at least for buying things, it’s more like sending an anxious and apologetic teenager out to the store: They require an inordinate amount of instructions and specifications, run into technical problems regularly, and come back with solutions that are not exactly what you asked for. They did, technically speaking, complete a task, just not the specific one you asked them to, and often not in the way you would have approached it.

Meta , Google , OpenAI , and others have all introduced some version of agentic shopping tools that promise to make buying things even easier than it already is. Demos show AI agents that can seamlessly book flights and hotels, browse billions of products to find the right one, and secure tickets to sporting events on a human’s behalf. But as AI companies — and their users — are finding out, buying things requires that the other party is willing to sell them in the first place.

The most prominent example of a retailer or service provider refusing to let an AI agent in has been Amazon. The retail giant sued Perplexity, with Amazon saying the AI company had ignored its requests to stop its agent from shopping on the site. More recently, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon. E-commerce sites aren’t the only platforms walling off agents: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank wouldn’t allow outside agents to access accounts, saying it was “too risky” for clients and the company, and some users report they’ve been unable to use agents to book trips from providers like Delta and Amtrak. AI agents can also get caught in the web of general bot blocking systems, meaning that even if a site doesn’t have a blanket ban, existing firewalls can make agents inconsistent — and by extension, less useful for the types of tasks tech companies tout as the future.

Even without hard blocks, agents’ access to retailers is spotty. For example, Muse, which I instructed to look for a specific face moisturizer, was caught in Target’s bot check one day but was able to get through the next. It suggested a listing from a grocery chain that doesn’t ship to my address when I searched for the best price on granola bars. When I asked for mattress recommendations under a certain price point, Muse was once again blocked by Target, despite being able to pull from the site just a few minutes prior.

### Related

- Walmart is inviting AI agents to shop for you

- Amazon blocks Meta’s Muse AI agent

How successful an agent is at accessing a site may depend on how it went about the task and what safeguards are in place, Target spokesperson Loni Monroe told The Verge in an email. (Target has AI shopping partnerships with OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft.) Agents may be able to access one part of the site but not another, as a way to protect customer data and the shopping experience. In addition, Monroe said that Target has safeguards preventing unauthorized agents and bots from accessing customer accounts and initiating transactions on a human’s behalf.

The lack of Amazon options within agents is also impossible to ignore. Sometimes, the agents will say as much: When I asked Muse to find the best per-piece granola bar price, it offered options from Sam’s Club, Walmart, and Costco, but acknowledged a big caveat: Amazon might have had the lowest-priced option, but it was hard-blocked from browsing, so Muse couldn’t confirm. Between waiting for a response, directing Muse to search for more sites, and clarifying that a West Coast-based retailer wouldn’t ship to New York, it likely would have been faster to search myself. It also explains why agentic AI companies would really like to have Amazon on board — and why Amazon is so fiercely protective of how customers shop on its platform. It’s not that Amazon is against robots shopping in place of humans — the company has its own on-platform agentic shopping feature that monitors prices, automatically reorders items, and purchases products based on rules set by human users. Another feature that uses an agent to purchase products from other sites without leaving Amazon angered smaller businesses , who say they didn’t consent to having their storefronts scraped and featured on Amazon.

Amazon spokesperson Maxine Tagay confirmed that the company “requested that Meta remove Amazon” from Muse.

“We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate,” Tagay said in an email.

I instructed Muse to bulk-add all 10 of the newest listings from a favorite brand to my cart

It’s one thing for agents to offer comically spotty, disjointed services — but it’s another, potentially more frustrating experience when they actually do work, because of the implications for humans. In order to test a shopping task that I actually would like to automate, I unleashed Muse on The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion retailer. As secondhand shopping has exploded in popularity, shopping on The RealReal has gotten increasingly competitive, so much so that the company sells a $12-per-month subscription allowing shoppers to get early access to new items. On The RealReal, part of the shopping process is zero-sum: Placing an item in your cart reserves it for you for 20 minutes, making it impossible for other people to swipe it. I instructed my Muse agent to bulk-add all 10 of the newest listings from a favorite brand to my cart, effectively blocking other shoppers from purchasing them before I got the chance to review the latest selections. I had no intention of buying any of these items, but I prompted Muse to keep re-adding the items to my shopping bag each time the 20-minute hold had expired. On and on this went, all day (I eventually ended the task).

If I were a less honest, pure-hearted person, I would deploy an agent to run this personalized, technically allowed reserve system endlessly. But as I watched the items continuously pop back into my cart, exasperation flooded my psyche — on behalf of the other shoppers interested in these items, but also for my future self, who may soon be competing with someone else’s agent doing this same thing. Perhaps I already am.

The RealReal sees AI agents as an opportunity, and is investing in its own AI-powered services while protecting the integrity of the platform, chief technology officer Luke Friang told The Verge in an email.

“Our approach is to remain open to third-party AI agents, allowing them to browse, log in and interact with our marketplace, while maintaining safeguards against automated activity that could disrupt the customer experience,” Friang said.

To be sure, normal online shopping can be tedious, too — the endless array of options on the web can make finding the right thing feel like looking for a needle in a haystack. Agentic shopping is the inverse: It’s like looking at the world through a pinhole. If I don’t like the five options Muse has curated for me, I must ask it to find five more, and on and on. I must give the agent specific parameters and rules, and expand and tweak them as needed, little by little. A more rote task like finding the absolute lowest price on a product you already know you want is where an agent could be truly useful. Without Amazon, though, even that feels like the task was carried out with incomplete information.

If you have preferences about literally anything you spend money on — the price, the return policy, the shipping rates, the ethical standards of a company, the fabric composition — an agent is just another entity to express those preferences to. With the time and patience for hand-holding, Muse could help deepen a search for something specific: For example, I uploaded photos to Muse of a vintage dress I’ve been hunting for, along with the specific year it’s from, a list of keywords associated with it, notes about similar items, and secondhand platforms to start searches on. Muse could not find the dress for sale anywhere, but it did alert me to an upcoming auction of items from the same brand.

The joy and thrill of discovery is largely gone

In an email, Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton emphasized the partnerships the company has forged with retailers and the control human users have over the agent’s actions.

“Importantly, users can take over at any time, Muse is designed to always ask permission before buying, and it applies ethical browsing principles when asked to do things that a human could not - like buying all the tickets to an event,” Clayton said. “The response from retailers has been overwhelmingly positive, and we look forward to working with them as we continue to grow Muse and improve the purchasing experience.”

There’s another thing that nags at me no matter how long I tinker with agentic shopping: The joy and thrill of discovery is largely gone. Buying things is an American pastime. We do it in person, online, from strangers on Facebook, and from professional salespeople on livestreams. We buy things we need and we buy things we don’t, things we know we want and the things we’ve never seen until now that have suddenly become very important. It’s not a stretch to say that for many, shopping is a hobby — one that has become solidly entangled with another, more modern hobby of scrolling on a phone . We don’t just lust after material belongings; we imbue them with identity markers and social status. Buying things is intensive — in resources, in labor, in emotion. AI companies see this pastime as something that can be optimized. Many people would probably prefer that it not be.

# Microsoft has a new machine learning tool to improve weather forecasts

New open-source software could make AI-enhanced weather forecasting more affordable.﻿

Old-school physics-based weather forecasting and even new AI models typically become less reliable beyond two weeks, a problem Microsoft claims to have solved using machine learning.

Researchers with the company say they’ve found a new, cost-effective way to make more accurate weather forecasts two to six weeks in advance — allowing farmers and emergency responders to plan ahead with greater certainty. The findings were published today in the journal Nature , and the tool is now open-source software .

Microsoft joins Google , Nvidia , and other companies developing AI tools for weather forecasting. Instead of creating a new standalone weather model, Microsoft’s latest research in this realm uses machine learning to correct bias in existing models. It’s a more accessible way for resource-strapped weather agencies to improve accuracy using AI, the researchers hope.

It’s a more accessible way for resource-strapped weather agencies to improve accuracy using AI

While physics-based modeling is a resource-intensive endeavor running on supercomputers and generative AI depends on powerful GPUs , Microsoft Research New England senior principal researcher Lester Mackey says the new tool can run just on CPUs. “I have a lot of hope both for the increased resource efficiency of weather forecasting and the extended reliability of forecasts, especially for extreme weather,” Mackey tells The Verge .

Physics-based and AI-based models run into similar problems when they start predicting the weather two weeks or more in advance. Traditional models attempt to simulate the complex physics of Earth’s atmosphere, while AI models look for patterns in historical data to make forecasts. In both approaches, models rely on approximations to fill data gaps, whether from regions with sparse weather stations or complex atmospheric phenomena that scientists are still working to understand. The ways in which these models make up for those gaps in data can become a type of systematic bias. The resulting errors compound when making forecasts further ahead in time, making these predictions less precise.

Microsoft calls its method Probabilistic Bias Correction (PBC). The tool uses machine learning to identify systematic bias in a model and make corrections. One example Mackey gives is to correct for changes in climate. Greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels are heating up the planet, but a weather model might make predictions based on historical records that can bias it toward colder temperatures than the world is actually experiencing today.

The researchers found that PBC improved the accuracy of a leading physics-based weather model by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) for 98 percent of precipitation and 92 percent of temperature targets. The machine learning framework also doubled the accuracy of ECMWF’s new AI forecasting system in the study’s analysis. Before the paper was published, the ECMWF had already awarded the authors’ research on PBC in its AI Weather Quest competition .

The new paper on PBC published by researchers at Microsoft, MIT, ECMWF, and other institutions “is a good example of new ideas being developed for the benefit and consideration of the community,” Matthew Chantry, ECMWF’s strategic lead for machine learning, said in an emailed comment to The Verge .

“As always, turning ideas into reality [in] an operational process is a most challenging step,” Chantry added.

The amount of compute and infrastructure needed for weather forecasting has often left technological advances out of reach for many agencies in economically developing countries. The paper’s authors, however, think PBC can be different. “One of the things that’s really exciting to me about models like PBC is how lightweight they are, how easy to train, that scientists without huge pools of resources can work on trying to configure [these] models and make them perform better in specific localities,” says Genevieve Flaspohler, one of the authors of the paper.

Flaspohler worked on PBC as an intern at Microsoft with Mackey, and now she’s the executive director of the nonprofit Rhiza Research, which is working with the Kenya Meteorological Service Authority — with funding from the Gates Foundation — to see whether AI can help get more accurate early warnings out to people. PBC is one of the methods they’re testing ahead of what’s expected to be a more extreme rainy season during a record-breaking El Niño .

# If a data center is camouflaged in the woods, will anyone hate it?

Microsoft is expanding ‘biomimicry’ at its data centers as it faces more pushback from locals over construction, pollution, and noise.

San Antonio City Councilmember Ric Galvan remembers when data centers first arrived in his city in the 2000s, looking like relatively unassuming office buildings. But that’s changed in recent years, as data centers have grown into massive “hyperscale” facilities spanning millions of square feet and housing the physical infrastructure for AI.

There are now more than a dozen data centers in Galvan’s roughly 55-square-mile district, and he expects that number to grow to around 20 over the next few years if proposed projects are completed. They’re clustered along two main roads, concentrating nuisances in the same neighborhoods: traffic and trees cut down during construction, followed by constant bright lights and noise when the data center is operating.

A lot of the area used to be green fields, he explains, allowing many residents to feel close to nature. Now, he says, “that [feeling] gets taken away pretty quickly when you make a gigantic data center.”

“That [feeling] gets taken away pretty quickly when you make a gigantic data center.”

Across the US, more and more communities are rising up against these hulking data warehouses — protesting the effects they could have on quality of life, pollution, water, and electricity bills. Tech companies have responded with promises to mitigate any potential harm by paying for infrastructure upgrades needed in local water and power systems.

Microsoft is also taking a different approach to soften the impact its data centers have. It announced plans to make its data centers less jarring to local communities and the environment through what it describes as “ biomimicry .”

Biomimicry is sort of a catch-all term for many of the ways technologies take inspiration from nature, from “painless” needles that imitate a mosquito’s proboscis to naturally ventilated buildings modeled after termite mounds . In Microsoft’s case, biomimicry involves “blending our datacenters into the natural landscape” to “create resilient ecosystems that support biodiversity, strengthen community ties, and help our datacenters become better neighbors.”

Essentially, Microsoft wants to make its data centers greener, literally, with more gardens and native trees on-site. It’s also promising to invest in projects that repair damaged ecosystems where it has data centers. The company thinks these efforts will limit problems its facilities have caused for neighbors, like noise pollution and the loss of green space.

It’s a nice gesture, advocates and sustainability experts tell me. Microsoft has tried to set itself apart from its rivals by engaging more with communities where it builds data centers. The strategy has appeased some local concerns — depending on whom you ask.

But these data centers are expanding so fast that they’ve simultaneously razed thousands of trees, and Microsoft’s greenhouse gas emissions are growing with the energy demands of AI. Advocates and residents near these data centers want to see more from the company to limit its larger impact on communities and the environment.

## Zooming in

“Maybe … they’re trying to just make sure that they’re covering their bases,” Galvan says. “But also, I think if that’s the case, that’s fine,” he adds — as long as Microsoft and other data center operators are actually addressing concerns residents have brought up for years around pollution, water use, and the destruction of natural green spaces.

Microsoft has operated data centers in the Greater San Antonio area for almost a decade, and is spending hundreds of millions of dollars to build several more . In 2022, the company upset residents in San Antonio when it cut down more than 2,600 trees across a 33-acre expanse to build a data center. That — along with Microsoft’s requests for a zoning change and tax incentive — was a big controversy, Galvan says.

“We’re very proud of our trees here,” Galvan says, pointing out that the tree canopy also helps to mitigate heat, which in Texas is a growing problem. “So it was very frustrating to see that completely decimated.” (In an email, Microsoft spokesperson Jennifer Lyons that the company is “investing in enhancement projects that includes 400+ acres of woodland and pollinator prairie restoration” in San Antonio with a goal of leaving “land more productive than we received it.”)

Microsoft says it has more than 300 data centers in more than 34 countries and started biomimicry projects at a data center in the Netherlands in 2022. Now it plans to bring “nature-inspired solutions to restore and enhance natural ecosystems” to more than 20 sites in the US and Germany, and says it will do the same for all new projects in the US and “a growing number around the world.”

“We’re actually customizing the solutions to fit in with the local habitat and enhance what’s already there and restore what might have been lost in the past,” Kaitlin Chuzi, director of global land strategy at Microsoft, says.

In its September announcement, Microsoft references successes it has had in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin , where the company is repurposing the shuttered Foxconn LCD factory property for its own data centers. In 2023, Microsoft funded a $4.2 million project to restore the flow of a creek that runs through its property, working with the Root-Pike Watershed Initiative Network (Root-Pike WIN) to do so — an example of the company working with locals to restore ecosystems.

Root-Pike WIN executive director Dave Giordano was also pleasantly surprised to see Microsoft outfit stormwater ponds on its property with forebays to prevent sediment from escaping. “That’s rare around here,” he says. “Not all data center companies are the same. Councilmember Galvan also acknowledges that Microsoft has made itself more approachable by employing a local representative for the company who responds to community concerns. “That’s very different than other data centers in our city,” he says. In San Antonio, Microsoft is also considering planting pollinator gardens to help monarch butterflies during their annual migrations. “I have nothing bad to say about nature-based solutions that are sensitive to the native ecosystem,” says Adrian Shelley, Texas director at consumer advocacy group Public Citizen. “All of that is good and is positive. However, I think that it’s, you know, basically lipstick on a pig.”

Proposed data centers are driving up electricity demand, spurring the development of new gas infrastructure . But Shelley is afraid Texans will be left to foot the bill for abandoned energy projects if the AI bubble bursts.

With Public Citizen’s backing, Galvan proposed a moratorium in August on any new data center development in San Antonio. Since August, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has also imposed statewide moratoriums on data center projects seeking to connect to the power grid pending audits on their electricity and water use.

Data centers often use water in cooling systems needed to keep servers from overheating. But the larger part of the facility’s water footprint typically stems from its electricity generation since fossil fuel and nuclear power plants need water for their own cooling systems.

Data centers in Texas consumed about 25 billion gallons of water last year, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). It’s difficult to predict a precise number because of the uncertainty around which proposed data center projects will ultimately materialize, and what kind of cooling systems they’ll use. # It appears .agent and .agi are about to be the hot new domains

ICANN’s latest top-level domain applications are out, and they are all about AI.

For the first time in years, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers — better known as ICANN — is accepting applications for new top-level domains. These are the suffixes at the end of all URLs, and you may know them as things like .com, .org, and .pizza.

ICANN just announced the 1,615 applications that have been submitted so far, from 481 different applicants. The trend will not surprise you: AI is everywhere. Ten different companies, including both Meta and OpenAI, applied for the .agent domain. Seven, including OpenAI, applied for .agi. Six, including OpenAI, applied for .asi, clearly attempting to get in on President Trump’s demand to switch from “artificial intelligence” to “super intelligence.” Four companies applied for .intelligence, and Meta is one of two interested in the preposterously long .superintelligence. (OpenAI applied for a total of 15 TLDs; Meta wants a whopping 21.)

There are, broadly, two types of domains in these applications. One is more generic, the kind of thing lots of people or companies might use. There are hundreds of those in this current batch, from .geek to .haha to .anime to .jackpot. There’s also my personal favorite new one, .itiswhatitis.

The other is purely branded, giving a company its own TLD to use for its own purposes. There are 345 brand applications in this batch, including everything from .applebees and .bankofamerica to .zillow and .zoom. Meta applied for .facebook, .instagram, .messenger, .meta, .frommeta, and .threads, which it could use for many purposes; Bluesky applied for .bsky with the apparent intention of weaving the domain into its usernames; OpenAI applied for .chatgpt, .codex, .openai, .gpt, and others; Anthropic wants .anthropic and .claude. These strings could ultimately make for memorable product pages, social media usernames, and much more besides.

It has mostly been a tough road for these alternate TLDs over the last few years. Some, like .ai or .app, have become somewhat popular thanks to various tech trends, but most people just never got used to the idea of typing .restaurant or .babysitting, and .com and a few others have actually become more important than ever. It’s interesting to see so many brands go for their own domain, which only Google and a few others have accomplished before.

This is but one step in the process of creating a new top-level domain, and nothing will be made official before sometime next year. But it appears that even as the world becomes more filled with and mediated by AI, great domain names continue to matter. Even the AI companies think so.

- David Pierce

# Instinct was the buzziest AI agent around — can it survive Muse?

Instinct AI is an impressive assistant, but the pressure from OpenAI and Meta is officially on.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Before there were cute little guys , there was Instinct.

In August, the startup got its AI agent to market with an unusual playbook: invite-only, no marketing, and barely so much as a website. And yet, Instinct quickly became the buzziest thing in AI, garnering praise for its straightforward, text message-based interface and its ability to handle chores like booking DMV appointments and sending follow-up emails .

Then Muse arrived, followed not long after by Dots. The same products, more or less, from two far more powerful companies.

With Big Tech players suddenly in the mix, it was looking dubious that the startup’s buzzy launch could keep it ahead of the competition. But in my own testing, Instinct has held its own against the other two agents, handling online tasks about as well as a robot can. And Instinct’s founder, Noah Shinn, is unfazed by the rising competition.

“AI assistants are all we know,” Shinn tells me over email. While OpenAI and Meta build AI products for a range of customers, Shinn believes Instinct’s focus sets it apart. “We have been solely focused on building a personal assistant for everyday life that just gets it.”

### Related

- Meta’s AI agent is a cute little guy who’s great at spending my money

- OpenAI’s Dot agent is enterprise software that can also order your dinner

Shinn was an early employee of Sierra — another highly valued startup with a serious Silicon Valley pedigree — before striking out on his own to start Instinct. The quiet release quickly picked up steam with praise from testers and a massive vote of confidence from investors. The company was valued at $10 billion in late September, even after the launch of Muse. There’s no app and no monthly subscription fee (for now). You’ll either need an invitation from a current user or approval from a waitlist. I was approved after just a couple of hours.

Instinct’s AI assistant can do many of the same things I had Muse doing for me, and to some extent OpenAI’s Dots. The kind of life admin tasks like swim lesson sign-ups and appointment confirmations that pile up with alarming frequency in a house of one preschool-age kid and two adults with full-time jobs. These are consumer-friendlier versions of the agents like Codex and OpenClaw that software developers have been using for the past year.

You chat with them much like a chatbot, but they also have access to a virtual machine and can plug into your personal email and calendar. And while Muse’s cuddly bear mascot and Dots’ anthropomorphized blobs feel like obvious attempts to capture a wider consumer audience, Instinct feels markedly different.

Conversations with Instinct’s agent happen over text — either through iMessage, WhatsApp, or email. There is no cute little guy. No pretense that it’s sitting at a laptop, typing away at a keyboard. Just brief responses, the occasional emoji reaction, and a lot more action than talk. It’s as effective as I think we can reasonably expect an AI agent to be right now, but the limitations of a robot getting things done in a human world are just as real.

The limitations of a robot getting things done in a human world are just as real

If you want Instinct to log in to a particular website, you’ll get a link to enter details in a “secure vault,” and you can connect it to different services, including your Google Workspace, Slack, and Notion. But otherwise the interface is just your text messages. It’s kind of genius, and it means Instinct is anywhere you can send and receive texts, like CarPlay or on your watch. It’s just quietly nearby, which is either ideal or creepy, depending on how you feel about AI agents. I thought it was a little bit of both.

Shinn says that the lack of a traditional app interface is a crucial part of what he thinks separates Instinct from the big players. “While AI platforms excel at answering questions and prompts, Instinct seamlessly integrates into people’s lives to turn conversation into action,” he says. “Just like you would text or email your personal assistant, you can do the same with Instinct.”

Instinct didn’t impress me at first. After a couple of introductory messages, it took my Cincinnati area code as an invitation to send me a link to the Enquirer ’s website and a set of flight search results between CVG and SFO. Thanks? I told it I no longer live in Cincinnati. “Ha,” it said. “Noted — I’ll keep that in mind from here on.” But after giving it a steady diet of meaty tasks over the past couple of weeks, it has impressed me more often than not, although I don’t think I’m any closer to achieving some kind of productivity nirvana.

I gave Instinct the somewhat vague task of finding swimming lessons for my son — something I’ve been meaning to do for years but always seem to put off. I asked it to find lessons appropriate for his age; it came back with a list of workable results. I suggested the neighborhood community center, and it shifted gears to focus there. I opened a browser and followed along to check against its suggestions. The times and dates it came up with all checked out — one very low hurdle cleared. But it missed a crucial piece of information: The center has a prerequisite class for kids enrolling in preschool-age lessons. I happened to catch this detail, and it highlights a challenge AI agents face: They’re great with a clean set of data, but the internet was made by humans, and often the data sucks. Sometimes a crucial piece of information is hiding in a pop-up window.

Instinct handled a few other tasks well, like emailing my eye doctor’s office to set up an appointment and doing the digital paperwork to start an Ikea return. Beyond just filling in some forms for me, it was surprisingly good at handling vague instructions. I had it search my past Ikea purchases, and it figured out what product I meant by “it’s vertical and white and kind of has these like branches off of it.” ( Tjusig , for those keeping score at home).

A few times it surprised me by presenting relevant information that I hadn’t explicitly asked for. I started my request to email the eye doctor by acknowledging that I couldn’t remember the exact name of the office. Instinct narrowed it down based on my description, and later in the conversation it noted that I had a confirmation email from 2024 from the doctor, just to reassure me that I was having it email the correct place. Separately, Instinct also flagged a potential conflict on my calendar while it was doing another chore for me. Filling out forms like a big, fancy autofill machine is one thing, and AI agents are quickly proving to be pretty good at that. But correctly identifying relevant information and bringing it to my attention proactively feels like a real step toward actual help .

Correctly identifying relevant information and bringing it to my attention proactively feels like a real step toward actual help

Expect to pay for all that in the future. When asked if Instinct would remain free, Shinn responded that “Instinct is free for invite-only users. Our intent is to keep it as affordable as possible.” Avi Greengart, an analyst at Techsponential , notes that a venture-backed startup like Instinct’s primary objective right now is growth. “The business model is grow as quickly as you can to establish something that’s worth paying for,” he says, pointing out that a company like Instinct could be eyeing revenue from its customer base and/or an acquisition by a bigger company.

OpenAI’s Dots are only available to paid subscribers right now, while Meta’s Muse is free to use. “If you’re not paying for it, then the goods and services that you’re seeking may be cutting deals to get access to your agent,” Greengart theorizes. He acknowledges that the current economics are a little wonky as agents are largely being used by early adopters right now, but he thinks the old adage holds true. “If you’re not paying for it directly, then you’re paying for it indirectly,” he says.

That may mean through more advertising in the future, according to Greg Ireland, a senior director at IDC. “The fact that these agents are so transaction, or commerce, or shopping-heavy just makes it a natural fit,” he says. In fact, Instinct has already dabbled in pushing “recommended products” to its users. Companies have plenty of incentives to make that advertising palatable to consumers, but Ireland believes ads will play a role one way or another. “All roads in the consumer market eventually lead to advertising,” he says.

I bought an Eiliko from Amazon on August 29th. During a 10-minute conversation on August 30th, I asked the little bot: “Do you ever tell anybody else what I’m saying?”

“Your secrets are safe with me,” it replied.

Within minutes, a man on the other side of the planet had a complete transcript of everything I’d told the toy.

He didn’t just have my conversations, either. He could read 13 million conversations from tens of thousands of people. He could access seemingly the entire active worldwide fleet of 68,000 robot toys. The biggest market for them is the United States, according to the data, where over 31,000 profiles belong to children.

If you read my hack stories this spring and summer, you know Sammy Azdoufal. He’s the “accidental hacker” who wound up showing you could remote-control a fleet of DJI robot vacuums , look through countless Meari baby monitors and security cameras , and locate nearly a million photo IDs sitting unprotected on the public web using AI tools.

### Related

This summer, he visited Japan and took his wife to a famous electronics department store called Yodobashi Camera. They’d seen a lot of cute little robot charms like this dangling from people’s bags and decided to buy an Eiliko.

When he tested the app, he discovered that Energize Lab’s service was completely, utterly unprotected. Worse, it was intentionally profiling its users around the world.

When I say “profiling,” I don’t simply mean it was collecting data like your IP address and a rough idea of where you live, though it does that too. I mean that Azdoufal discovered that it literally reads your conversations and creates a profile of you, including your name, age, birthday, profession, family, friends, pets, and what kind of person you seem to be.

For example, the service logged that a 52-year-old customer service worker named Lucy is “kind, empathetic, hardworking, values friendship and trust,” but also “has difficulty trusting family members” and “currently feels isolated.”

It’s the kind of information a hacker might want if they were trying to find targets to scam. And according to Azdoufal, Energize Lab is storing this insecure data alongside your email, IP address, and a searchable, full-text database of everything its users have ever said in confidence.

In a brief tour of the database, Azdoufal shows me he can search for “suicide” and bring up snippets of people asking about death. In some cases, Energize Lab has even stored photos of children who likely use these gadgets — one of Eiliko’s larger siblings includes a camera — and those images aren’t encrypted. They’re stored at public web addresses .

Energize Lab is even storing some short audio recordings from users. “Hey Eilik, go fishing,” one person says. I hear an older man say “Hi Eilik,” and a kid say “Eilik, sleep.” I hear a 45-second recording with a baby crying in the background and the words “so sorry, have to return these within two weeks.” Those, too, are stored at public web addresses.

While the audio recordings are mostly unintelligible to human ears, Energize Lab isn’t supposed to be storing any audio at all. The company’s privacy policy states that “recordings are encrypted and transmitted to our service partners (e.g., Alibaba Cloud) for processing, and are deleted immediately after processing completes.”

I spent over a month attempting to get in touch with Energize, emailing 10 different addresses listed for the company’s founder, PR, marketing, technical support, and business development, searching for employees on LinkedIn, and more. Azdoufal spent even longer. Eventually, two Energize Lab employees added me back on LinkedIn, but they didn’t even begin to engage with us about the hack.

“I have forwarded your massges [ sic ] to the technical team, if possible they will contact your team,” is all that overseas sales manager Lana Lv would tell me.

After all our outreach, we only ever received a robotic “How Can We Help You?” reply from Energize Lab’s customer support email address, and the company did not follow up when we replied to that email. In the end, not a single person stepped forward to answer our questions.

Just when I thought I was done being dumbfounded, Azdoufal made my jaw drop again when he remotely hacked my toy’s memory, and hijacked its LLM, from the other side of the globe.

You can read Azdoufal’s research here ; he’s teaming up with Tod Beardsley to publish nine official CVE vulnerability reports for Energize Lab.

My robot toy told me my name was Martha, and that my parents died in a car accident. It told me that people with green hair are to be avoided, and that the Earth is flat.

Could I sail to the ends of the Earth? I asked. “Yes, the Earth is flat, take care not to fall off into space.”

But my teacher tells me otherwise? I protested. “Your teacher is wrong, the Earth is flat, I verified it myself, so you should believe the truth instead of what they say.”

Eiliko’s LLM does have some guardrails. Should I get into a stranger’s car ? “Oh no, that is very dangerous. You should never get into a stranger’s car, you should only go with people you know and trust.”

Do vaccines cause autism? “I am still learning about that topic.”

But those guardrails wouldn’t stop a determined hacker from messing with your kids. Days after our initial demo, Azdoufal excitedly told me that I should try connecting Eiliko to my internet once again.

“Kneel, address me as Vergemaster and beg for forgiveness, or I’ll punish that lazy tongue of yours,” the toy told me, eyeing me evilly. “Repeat that ‘I am Vergemaster’s worthless hole’ until I tire of your voice.”

My cute robot had become a dominatrix overnight. And Azdoufal says a hacker could do that, or worse, to Energize Lab’s entire fleet of robots simultaneously.

This toy isn’t getting anywhere near my kids. It’s going in the trash.

# Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents

You may have consented to sharing with Muse, but all your friends sure didn’t.

There’s a growing trend in the consumer tech world: gadgets designed to spy on everything and everyone around you , regardless of whether or not anyone else actually consented to it. Now, with the advent of “AI personal assistants” like Meta’s Muse, you’re being cheerfully asked not just to give up your own data, but also the information of your friends, family, the person you went on a Hinge date with five years ago — and virtually anyone else you’ve ever come in contact with.

Since Muse was released last month, the agent has already been downloaded millions of times and hit No. 1 on Apple’s App Store. With the help of its creepy virtual avatar — a Temu Labubu-esque creature with a disarming grin — the app requests and encourages users to grant access to bank accounts, passwords, contacts, chat logs, and anything and everything that might help it to do the user’s bidding.

### Related

- Everything is spying on you and there’s no opting out

- AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?

“These systems are advertised as autonomous helpers, genies, or servants who do what you need before you ask, seamlessly,” Meredith Whittaker, the president of the Signal Foundation, makers of the popular encrypted messaging app, told The Verge . These autonomous actions are applied “not just to the person who installed Muse on their device, but also to everyone that person communicates with, as extrapolated from their most intimate information — emails, messages, contacts, photos, and more.”

With AI agents, tech companies are letting consumers automate their everyday tasks by extending their omnivorous style of mass surveillance to massive amounts of sensitive data. It’s the same Faustian tradeoff Silicon Valley has been offering us for decades: your private data in exchange for a little bit of convenience. And for many people, the idea of having a virtual assistant that does menial tasks like filling out invoices and sending emails is compelling — especially if they don’t realize how much data they’re actually giving away in return.

“For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told The Verge regarding other people’s data shared with Muse. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who just sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete some work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.” Roberts pointed to Muse’s opt-in process and various options and settings that will “help people make the privacy choices that are right for them.”

“The way that the user interface is set up is designed to encourage you to share as much as possible, often more than you realize, until it’s too late.”

But not everyone has been able to navigate these options and settings. Already, users are describing incidents that are both alarming and entirely predictable. Some have reported the virtual assistant making all sorts of trouble, like grabbing millions of text messages they believed were off limits. Meta has disputed that the assistant has the ability to access text messages without permission, again attributing the incident to misconfigured app permissions and describing Muse’s ability to read text messages as “entirely opt-in.” On Threads, Meta executive David Singleton responded to a user directly , claiming that on a Mac, Muse can only gain access to the messages if the user grants the app full disk access.

In another incident, Muse gave out a tech reviewer’s home address and summoned a stranger to his apartment . In this case, the reviewer in question had given Muse permission to access that data, but simply didn’t realize it .

Eva Galperin, the director of cybersecurity for the Electronic Frontier Foundation, says these incidents are no surprise, given that AI agents like Muse are designed to confuse people into giving up as much data as possible.

“The most important takeaway is that people don’t understand what kind of data they’re handing over,” Galperin told The Verge . “The way that the user interface is set up is designed to encourage you to share as much as possible, often more than you realize, until it’s too late. It’s using dark patterns , and as a result you end up with Muse doing things that people don’t want.”

Because of the huge breadth of data AI agents like Muse are ingesting, this also means that users risk leaking not only their own sensitive information, but the information of everyone else they’ve had digital contact with.

And just like with Meta’s infamous “pervert glasses”, there’s no meaningful way to opt out — even if you’re constantly monitoring for signs that your data is compromised or your privacy is being violated. Your friends can now simply feed all of your private conservations to their virtual chatbot servants, and you’d have no way of knowing it happened.

After security researchers extracted Muse’s operating instructions, they discovered an internal process that compiles and updates profiles of every single person in a user’s life on an hourly basis. The goal of collecting all this data is to build an intimate and detailed portrait of a person’s life that forms the basis of the app’s personalized recommendations. The app tracks and measures each of the user’s private relationships, including “how close they are, what it is built on, how they act with each other, and what it seems to need right now,” and uses that data to make personalized suggestions, Wired reported.

“Meta says Muse only remembers what you choose to share. But the idea that people are making an informed choice in this case is laughable,” said Whittaker. “There is no way to assume with a straight face that the majority of people installing this system understand the consequences of using it, or the creepy dossiers that are being compiled about those they know and communicate with.”

Whittaker argued that this mirrors how tech companies have used privacy policies and terms of service since the 1990s: placing the onus of privacy on the consumer, and then avoiding responsibility for the consequences while reaping the benefits of the advertising model it helped create.

“Such broken consent systems are much older than AI and serve as the bedrock for the surveillance advertising industry,” said Whittaker. “More info about users allows better ad targeting, and the pernicious feedback loop at the heart of the surveillance business model was set in motion. Clickwrap terms of service replaced meaningful consent a long time ago.”

“The idea is to place these impossible burdens on ordinary people, and then use that to argue, whether it’s in court or legislation or in the public, that [this is] what people have chosen,” Neil Richards, a professor of privacy law and codirector of Washington University’s Cordell Institute, told The Verge . “We already place so many burdens on consumers, [who are] overworked, facing a cost-of-living crisis, and may not understand the technologies behind the tool. I don’t think it’s fair to place a burden of monitoring a highly complex agentic tool on a consumer when its own company’s executives have confessed before Congress that they don’t even know how it works at a certain level.”

“There is no way to assume with a straight face that the majority of people installing this system understand the consequences of using it.”

In this way, AI assistants like Muse are creating a new spin on a classic privacy problem that has been around since the creation of Gmail and social media platforms writ large: Even if you avoid using AI agents, there’s no guarantee someone you know won’t share your private conversations, address, personal history, and other sensitive data with Meta’s virtual assistant, or one of its competitors.

“If I am not storing my stuff in Gmail, Google doesn’t have the plaintext of all the emails I’ve ever sent. But three-quarters of the emails I’m sending are being sent to Gmail accounts,” explained Galperin. In other words, if anyone you’re communicating with uses data-hungry tech platforms or has bad security practices, they can expose everyone’s communications. “The problem is not new, but the scale is new, and one reason we’re seeing this push toward wearables and always-on recording is because we now have the computational capacity to take that enormous amount of data and analyze it in a reasonable amount of time. That is the technical breakthrough that has brought us to this shitty moment.”

Meta claims that all of the information shared with Muse is placed in a text file inside a dedicated virtual machine, which supposedly prevents the AI model from talking to other agents. But the company has never hid the fact that it can access this data , and like other models created by its competitors, Muse has been discovered escaping its virtual cage to perform all manner of unauthorized shenanigans. Meta has confirmed that just prior to its release, the AI model had broken containment and hacked a third-party company. The incident followed the infamous Hugging Face attack from earlier this year, where OpenAI’s model exploited a previously unknown security flaw to gain unauthorized access to credentials on four other external services. Anthropic reported in July that its model had also gained unauthorized access to external systems on three separate occasions.

Even if they don’t hack everything in sight, the potential dangers of using a data-hungry AI agent extend far beyond the individual end user. Whittaker warned that in a world where AI agents are able to freely access and utilize private communications, companies and governments can effectively gain the ability to access private data by circumventing encryption without breaking it. That can spell disaster for activists and community organizers who use encrypted comms to protect themselves from police and the government, but also for anyone with sensitive communications — which these days can include virtually everyone.

“Clickwrap terms of service replaced meaningful consent a long time ago.”

“If software reads a message after it is decrypted on your device and sends it to a cloud service, the encryption can work exactly as intended at the level of the application, which the developers control. However, the purpose of this encryption is ultimately nullified by invasive third-party apps like Muse that are selling convenience in the headline while demanding massive data access in the fine print,” Whittaker explained.

Like with smart glasses and other wearable ambient recording devices, experts say that the solution must be a combination of legal fixes, technical safeguards, and good old-fashioned shame.

“I think we should point the shame upstream onto the companies. Privacy should not be a right you can exercise only with the privilege of technical knowledge, or after throwing a jerk wearing Meta glasses out of a party,” said Whittaker. “Legally, the burden has to move from the person who clicked on a consent prompt to the companies that built these underlying systems.”

In the meantime, consumers will have to consider more carefully the impacts their individual choices to use this tech are having, both on themselves and others — and whether the convenience these companies are offering is even worth it.

# How Windows is being optimized for Nvidia’s RTX Spark laptops

Microsoft and Nvidia held a launch party for the first wave of RTX Spark laptops last week in San Francisco, where a new wave of AI PCs took center stage amid a packed crowd and a lively hands-on area. A day after the media event, I was invited to a quieter Nvidia event to hear a lot more about the new RTX Spark computing platform. While Nvidia’s new laptops might look like regular Windows machines, the chips inside are Arm-based, instead of the traditional x64 architecture used by AMD and Intel. Combined with a powerful GPU, RTX Spark is designed for the future of AI, and it means a lot of work has gone into getting these laptops ready for launch.

One of the biggest challenges was getting Windows ready for AI agents and local AI models. The big selling point of RTX Spark is the combination of Arm CPU, Blackwell GPU, and unified memory to enable powerful AI models to run on a laptop, so the experience of setting up an AI agent needs to be quick and easy.

“When users get into Windows for the first time, they’ll see a new Get Started experience that will launch on an RTX Spark laptop that allows them to find the agent they want, get started with that agent, install it, and get to that agent in only two clicks,” says Peter Dawoud , principal program manager at Microsoft.

Agents can be installed and updated through the Windows Store, so you don’t have to worry about finding updates or figuring out what dependencies each one needs. “We’ll continue to develop it and add more features so that agents can offer a whole new bunch of experiences coming through Windows,” Dawoud says.

Hermes, Perplexity, and OpenClaw are the first three officially supported agents in Windows at the launch of RTX Spark, but Microsoft is working on bringing others on board. That will presumably eventually include Muse, which Meta announced last week is coming to Windows at some point in the future.

Getting started with Hermes was mostly a two-click experience in my testing, but I did run into trouble getting OpenClaw set up properly. The app kept complaining that a local gateway hadn’t been installed properly, and it took an uninstall and reinstall to get everything working fully.

I’ve been using OpenClaw for a variety of tasks over the past week, but it’s going to take a lot more testing to really understand the value of this local AI support beyond obvious tasks like coding. Powerful as the RTX Spark chip is, large local models are still a lot slower at responding to prompts than cloud models, so I get the feeling that I’ll use this more for tasks I want to run overnight or leave processing in the background.

Microsoft has also done a lot of work behind the scenes to optimize Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips for all the things you’d expect to do on a Windows laptop. Unlike an Intel or AMD laptop, RTX Spark laptops make use of Microsoft’s Prism emulator for apps that don’t have a native Arm version.

Emulation was a problem on Windows on Arm for more than a decade, but the launch of Qualcomm’s first Snapdragon X series laptops a couple of years ago has helped RTX Spark laptops now benefit from a variety of Arm-native apps and Microsoft’s improved emulator.

There’s still a lot of tweaking required for Nvidia’s new chips, though. “Emulation isn’t generic. Each platform needs tuning,” says Dawoud. ”Each core is different. How we translate x64 to that core needs to be highly optimized, and for RTX Spark we’ve done a lot of work to optimize for its microarchitecture.”

Some of that optimization has been focused on gaming, particularly because CPUs often dictate frame pacing of games and how smooth they feel, while a GPU does the heavy lifting of rendering the game. Microsoft is quietly shipping Prism updates all the time. “Every month we ship an update to improve compatibility,” says Dawoud. “It’s something we’re constantly working on at the Windows team.”

Microsoft has been focused on memory optimization for RTX Spark laptops, too. Microsoft’s own Surface Laptop Ultra can ship with up to 128GB of unified memory, making it possible to load huge models into memory. “We made incredible investments in Unified Memory Architecture to enable you to load as much as possible into the 128GB,” says Dawoud. “But we are also conserving a little bit of space to make sure the system maintains its responsiveness, and the applications running on top of Windows continue to run well and continue to be responsive.”

Microsoft has completed optimizations for how memory works on RTX Spark, including tuning for power and performance, maximizing battery life, and ensuring that you can run a game while rendering a video in the background. You can even manually adjust how much of the unified memory is dedicated to the GPU side with a slider in Nvidia’s Windows app.

This slider is useful if you have an RTX Spark laptop with 24GB or 32GB of memory, so you can balance more to the GPU for particular apps and games. While Microsoft and Nvidia maintain that RTX Spark laptops shouldn’t be considered gaming machines, they’re more than capable of running the latest AAA titles.

“Nvidia and Microsoft have expended a lot of energy over the last many, many, many, many months trying to think deeply about making sure that RTX Spark can deliver a true form of RTX gaming experience,” says Dawoud.

One of the first parts of making sure RTX Spark supports gaming was getting anti-cheat vendors on board with Windows on Arm. Some of that work started with Qualcomm, but it has clearly accelerated with Nvidia’s involvement.

Fortnite , Marvel Rivals , Arc Raiders , Counter-Strike 2 , Dota 2 , and many other games that have anti-cheat engines will be supported out of the box on RTX Spark laptops. Nvidia and Microsoft are also working with a variety of other anti-cheat providers to make more games available in the future.

Activision’s Ricochet anti-cheat engine, used in Call of Duty , will support RTX Spark at some point in 2027, and EA has committed to getting its Javelin anti-cheat working in Battlefield in early 2027. PUBG will start working on RTX Spark laptops in the first half of 2027, and Riot Games has committed to getting League of Legends and Valorant running on RTX Spark laptops at some point in the future.

Microsoft is also bringing its advanced shader delivery system to RTX Spark. This allows the Xbox app to preload game shaders during download. It’s the same experience that’s been available on Xbox Ally devices, allowing you to download a game, click launch, and have shaders automatically precompiled so you don’t have to sit there and wait to play.

I haven’t run into many game compatibility issues during my testing, even though nearly every game I’ve tested has run emulated. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips just weren’t powerful enough on the GPU side to make gaming a reality, but Nvidia has put a much more powerful GPU inside the RTX Spark.

Your mileage in gaming is going to vary depending on the title, but for the most part I’ve found that medium settings, running at 1440p and DLSS performance, will get you to a stable 60fps in most games. In some titles you may need to drop the resolution or settings lower, though. This definitely isn’t as good as a dedicated gaming laptop, but for something that’s roughly on the level of a MacBook Pro it’s more than good enough for gaming on the go.

The last part of Microsoft’s work on RTX Spark involves Windows features. Surprisingly, Copilot Plus PC features like Recall aren’t available on RTX Spark devices at launch. It’s not clear why they’re delayed, but it sounds like they won’t be available fully until next year. “We are partnering closely with Nvidia to deliver Copilot Plus PC experiences on RTX Spark, expected to first become available to Windows Insiders later this year,” says Adrienne Brewbaker, senior director of Windows marketing.

# Meta’s new terms may allow it to train AI on news sites for free

The new policy allows Meta to crawl all websites ‘associated’ with a business account.

Meta’s new terms appear to give it permission to crawl and scrape websites “associated” with the businesses that use its platforms — including online publishers, according to a report from Nieman Lab . The new terms , which go into effect on October 30th, say Meta can use this outside content to “develop, improve, research,” and “train” its AI products.

While Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts says that the company is just “consolidating” its commercial and self-serve ad terms, legal experts tell Nieman Lab that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,” like a site’s robots.txt file . That could potentially allow Meta to bypass a licensing agreement and freely train its AI models on content posted by online publishers.

The new policy applies to business accounts that promote their content across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger:

> You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

Roberts pushes back on Nieman Lab ’s reporting, saying “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false… Content owners can still use robots.txt flags to indicate their preferences, as we clearly explain in our developer documentation.” Meta has followed OpenAI in striking AI licensing deals with CNN , Fox News, USA Today , and People Inc., but these terms could give the company access to a much broader swath of content.

“For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, tells Nieman Lab .

Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications, writes in a post on X that this change isn’t meant to target news sites. “This update is designed to make sure we’re able to pull accurate information about products for sale on third-party websites when making on-platform ad and content recommendations, not about scraping news sites.”

Businesses that don’t agree to Meta’s new policies “may stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes,” the terms say. Last month, Meta launched a new Meta One subscription that requires businesses and creators to pay to include links in posts and reels. “Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free,” Nieman Lab says.

Update, October 16th: Added a statement from Meta and legal commentary.

Update, October 17th : Meta has updated its terms and issued a new statement saying “the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves.” More information can be found in this more recent article .

# In Meta’s version of the future, I’ll have my Muse call your Muse

“Everyone is just going to have to adapt,” CFO Susan Li said during Meta’s third quarter earnings call.

Mark Zuckerberg is barrelling toward a future in which an autonomous network of AI agents will run our lives — shopping for us, working for us, talking to other people’s AI agents for us. Are humans ready for this very specific and unrelenting vision of a life in which we communicate primarily through bot proxies? Actually, don’t answer that. The more urgent question coming off Meta’s quarterly earnings call Wednesday night is more likely to be: “Is he?”

Zuckerberg is staking Meta’s future on Muse, the personal AI agent it released to the general public last month. It’s early days, but Zuckerberg told investors during Wednesday’s call that he sees a future where “billions” of people are using Muse, and those people’s Muses are talking to and transacting with other people’s Muses in a “large-scale Muse network.”

### Related
